questions.q: Why is running a container process as root a security concern?
options: Root processes always run noticeably slower than non-root ones
Docker refuses to start any container running as root
If an attacker breaks out of a container running as root, they're much closer to compromising the host itself
Root containers cannot use volumes at all
questions.explain: A container running as root means a container breakout hands an attacker root on the host too -- running as a non-root user removes that direct escalation path.

questions.q: What does USER node in a Dockerfile do?
options: Renames the resulting container to 'node'
Creates a new Docker Hub account named node
Switches the container's running process to the non-root node user instead of the default root
Installs Node.js inside the image
questions.explain: USER sets which user the container's process runs as; the official Node image already includes a non-root node user for exactly this purpose.

questions.q: What does the --read-only flag (or read_only: true in compose) do to a container?
options: Makes the container's entire filesystem read-only except explicitly mounted volumes or tmpfs paths
Makes the underlying image permanently immutable on Docker Hub
Prevents the container from ever being stopped once started
Prevents the container from exposing any ports
questions.explain: --read-only mounts the container's filesystem read-only, so a compromised process can't rewrite application files on disk -- writable paths must be explicit volumes or tmpfs mounts.

options: It disables all networking for the container
It has no real effect -- capabilities only apply inside Kubernetes, not plain Docker
It grants full root privileges plus unrestricted network access
It strips every Linux capability from the container, then adds back only the one specific capability actually needed, following least privilege
questions.explain: Root's privileges are a bundle of discrete capabilities. Dropping all of them and adding back only what's genuinely required limits what a compromised process can do.

questions.q: Why might Northbridge prefer a minimal or distroless base image over a full ubuntu image for a production service?
options: Minimal images automatically encrypt all network traffic
Minimal images build faster but are otherwise identical in every way that matters for security
Full ubuntu images can never be configured to run as non-root
Fewer installed packages and no shell mean a smaller attack surface -- less for an attacker to exploit even with code execution inside the container
questions.explain: A minimal image has fewer tools (often no shell or package manager), which gives an attacker who achieves code execution far less to work with.
